name: unzip1
summary: The first element of every row, gathered into one list.
explanation: Data arrives in rows and gets consumed in columns. A list of records is a list of rows; the thing you actually want is often one field across all of them -- every id, every timestamp, every name. unzip1 is that projection for the first field: it takes a list of lists and hands back a list of their heads. It is exactly (map car rows) and it is named because the operation deserves a name, and because it is the one-column member of a family that goes up to five, so code that starts by pulling one column can grow to pull three without changing shape. The verb makes a real demand on its input: every row must have a first element. A row that is empty is not a row with a missing value, it is an error, and unzip1 says so rather than quietly producing a hole in the middle of a column.

examples.note: (1 2 3) -- the first column, lifted out of three rows.
(names (ann bo cy) empty () ragged (1 2 3)) -- rows may have different lengths, since only the head is read.

examples.code:
(define log '((login 09) (write 12) (login 15) (logout 19)))
(define kinds (unzip1 log))
(display (list 'kinds kinds
               'distinct (delete-duplicates kinds)
               'logins (length (filter (lambda (k) (eq? k 'login)) kinds))))
(newline)
examples.note: (kinds (login write login logout) distinct (login write logout) logins 2) -- one projection, then ordinary list work on the column.

caveats: Every row must be non-empty. (unzip1 '((1) ())) raises rather than putting a hole in the column.
Rows longer than one element are fine -- the extra fields are ignored, not an error.
It is (map car rows), so it allocates a fresh list. The elements are shared, the spine is not.
It answers ONE list, not a value bundle. unzip2 and up answer multiple values and need call-with-values or define-values.
On an empty list of rows it answers the empty list, which is the right identity but means an all-empty result cannot be told from no input.
usecases: Pulling one field out of a list of records before sorting, counting, or summing it.
Recovering the keys of an association list represented as two-element lists rather than pairs.
The first step of a column-wise transformation, where the rest of the row is not needed.

learn.concept: Rows and columns are two readings of the same nested list, and projecting between them is a verb rather than a loop.
learn.progression: Write (map car rows) and see it works. Then write it again for the second column and notice you now need cadr. Then discover unzip2 gives you both at once, and that unzip1 was the shape you had already been writing by hand.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (ids-in orders) (unzip1 orders))
(define batch '((1001 shipped) (1002 held) (1003 shipped)))
(display (list 'all (ids-in batch)
               'one (ids-in '((2001 held)))
               'none (ids-in '())))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (x-coords points) (unzip1 points))
(define (span pts) (let ((xs (x-coords pts))) (- (apply max xs) (apply min xs))))
(display (map span '(((0 0) (3 4) (7 1)) ((5 5) (5 9)) ((2 0) (9 0) (4 0) (1 0)))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A fulfilment report needs every order id from a list of (id status) rows. Candidates: unzip1 (says exactly what it does, refuses an empty row, and is the same call shape you will use when the report grows a second column), (map car rows) (identical result, but car reads as a cons operation rather than a field projection, and it says nothing about what column 1 means), (map first rows) (better named, still one column and still not the family), a named let accumulating heads (three lines to say map), assoc-based lookup (wrong verb entirely -- it searches for a key, it does not project a column). unzip1 is the pick because a report that pulls one column today pulls two tomorrow.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: order ids from a full batch, a single-row batch, and an empty one, so the identity case is shown rather than assumed. math: x-coordinates projected out of point lists and turned into a horizontal span, over three point sets including one that is entirely flat. cs: the projection applied to a square table, a ragged one where rows have different lengths, and a nested one where the first field is itself a list -- which shows that unzip1 reads exactly one level deep.
row-2-audit.meta: The ragged case in the cs program is the one that matters. unzip1 does not require a rectangular table, only that column zero exists, and that is a weaker and more useful contract than it first appears.
row-2-audit.eng: Projecting a column by name rather than by accessor is what lets the row layout change without every caller changing with it.
row-2-audit.math: The span of a point set along one axis is a projection followed by a reduction. Separating the two is what lets the same reduction serve any axis.
row-2-audit.cs: A column projection that reads one level deep composes with itself: apply it twice and you have the first field of the first field, which is how nested records get flattened.

row-3-dimension.setup: Taking the first field out of every row of a table.

rungs.domain: a week of daily rainfall readings tagged with the station that took them
rungs.code:
(define week '((mon 0) (tue 4) (wed 12) (thu 0) (fri 3) (sat 0) (sun 8)))
(define days (unzip1 week))
(define (wet-days rows)
  (let loop ((d (unzip1 rows)) (r rows) (out '()))
    (cond ((null? r) (reverse out))
          ((> (cadr (car r)) 0) (loop (cdr d) (cdr r) (cons (car d) out)))
          (else (loop (cdr d) (cdr r) out)))))
(display (list 'days days 'wet (wet-days week) 'dry (- (length days) (length (wet-days week)))))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a symbol table where the projected column becomes the key index for a second pass
rungs.code:
(define table '((x int) (y string) (z int) (w bool)))
(define (index-of name tbl)
  (let loop ((names (unzip1 tbl)) (i 0))
    (cond ((null? names) #f)
          ((eq? (car names) name) i)
          (else (loop (cdr names) (+ i 1))))))
(define (resolve name tbl)
  (let ((i (index-of name tbl)))
    (if i (list name 'at i 'type (cadr (list-ref tbl i))) (list name 'unbound))))
(display (map (lambda (n) (resolve n table)) '(x z q)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare numbers it is a projection and the result is the whole answer. On the rainfall week the projected column is walked IN LOCKSTEP with the original rows -- days and readings advance together, so the column is not the answer but the label supply for a filter driven by a different column. In the symbol table the projection becomes an index: the position of a name in the projected column is the position of its row in the table, so one unzip1 turns a linear search over names into a row lookup by number, and the type is read from the row the index found. The verb never changes; what climbs is whether the column is the output, a parallel track, or an address.
row-3-dimension.meta: Rung three depends on a property the first two do not use: unzip1 preserves order, so index i in the column is row i in the table. Any projection that sorted or deduplicated would break the lookup silently.
row-3-dimension.eng: Labelling a filtered result requires keeping the labels aligned with the data. Walking two lists in step is the cheapest way, and it works because the projection did not reorder anything.
row-3-dimension.math: Counting the complement rather than filtering twice is one traversal instead of two, and it is exact because the two sets partition the week.
row-3-dimension.cs: A symbol table lookup is a search in the name column followed by an index into the rows. That is what every real implementation does, with a hash instead of a scan.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (matches-map-car? rows) (equal? (unzip1 rows) (map car rows)))
(display (map matches-map-car? '(((1 2) (3 4)) ((9)) () ((1) (2 3) (4 5 6)) (((a) b)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (length-preserved? rows) (= (length (unzip1 rows)) (length rows)))
(display (map length-preserved? '(() ((1)) ((1 2) (3 4)) ((1) (2) (3) (4) (5)) ((a b c)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (round-trips? col rest)
  (let ((rows (map (lambda (a b) (list a b)) col rest)))
    (equal? (unzip1 rows) col)))
(display (map (lambda (p) (round-trips? (car p) (cdr p)))
              (list (cons '(1 2 3) '(a b c)) (cons '() '()) (cons '(9) '(z))
                    (cons '(#f #f) '(1 2)) (cons '(x) '((nested list))))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: unzip1 is exactly (map car rows); it returns one element per row, so length is preserved; and it inverts the construction of two-element rows, recovering the original first column unchanged including when that column contains #f or nested lists.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all lists of non-empty rows r: unzip1(r) = map(car, r); |unzip1(r)| = |r|; and for any lists a and b of equal length, unzip1(map(list, a, b)) = a
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: the definitional identity, the length law, and the round trip. What would falsify them: a disagreement with map car on ragged input, a result shorter than the input because some row was skipped, or a round trip that lost an element because #f was treated as absence. The #f column in the third program is there for exactly that -- a projection that used a falsy sentinel internally would drop those rows.
row-4-proof.eng: Length preservation is what makes it safe to walk the column alongside the rows. If the projection could skip a row, every lockstep loop built on it would desynchronise.
row-4-proof.math: unzip1 is a left inverse of the two-column zip, not a two-sided one -- it discards the second column. A left inverse is enough to recover what you put in.
row-4-proof.cs: Agreement with map car is the specification. Stating it as a checkable property rather than a comment is what keeps an optimised implementation honest.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (keys-of rows) (unzip1 rows))
(define (group-by-key rows)
  (let loop ((ks (keys-of rows)) (r rows) (acc '()))
    (if (null? r)
        (map (lambda (p) (cons (car p) (reverse (cdr p)))) (reverse acc))
        (let* ((k (car ks))
               (hit (assq k acc)))
          (loop (cdr ks) (cdr r)
                (if hit
                    (map (lambda (p) (if (eq? (car p) k) (cons k (cons (cadr (car r)) (cdr p))) p)) acc)
                    (cons (cons k (list (cadr (car r)))) acc)))))))
(display (group-by-key '((fruit apple) (veg leek) (fruit pear) (veg kale) (fruit fig))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (axis rows) (unzip1 rows))
(define (deltas rows)
  (let loop ((xs (axis rows)) (out '()))
    (if (or (null? xs) (null? (cdr xs)))
        (reverse out)
        (loop (cdr xs) (cons (- (cadr xs) (car xs)) out)))))
(define (monotone? rows) (let ((d (deltas rows))) (or (null? d) (every (lambda (n) (>= n 0)) d))))
(display (list 'deltas (deltas '((0 a) (3 b) (7 c) (8 d)))
               'up (monotone? '((0 a) (3 b) (7 c)))
               'down (monotone? '((0 a) (9 b) (2 c)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (tags rows) (unzip1 rows))
(define (histogram rows)
  (let loop ((t (tags rows)) (acc '()))
    (if (null? t)
        (sort acc (lambda (a b) (string<? (symbol->string (car a)) (symbol->string (car b)))))
        (let ((hit (assq (car t) acc)))
          (loop (cdr t)
                (if hit
                    (cons (cons (car t) (+ 1 (cdr hit))) (remove (lambda (p) (eq? (car p) (car t))) acc))
                    (cons (cons (car t) 1) acc)))))))
(display (list 'counts (histogram '((get 1) (post 2) (get 3) (get 4) (put 5)))
               'single (histogram '((only 0)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: unzip1 lifts the first field out of every row, in order and one per row.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: keys-of is one call; group-by-key walks the key column in lockstep with the rows and buckets each row's second field under its first, which is a relational group-by built from one projection and an association list. math: axis is one call; deltas turns the projected column into its successive differences and monotone? then answers whether the table is sorted on that column -- a property of the table derived entirely from one of its columns. cs: tags is one call; histogram counts occurrences in the projected column and sorts the result, which is the whole of a request-method breakdown or any other frequency report.
row-5-emergence.meta: All three compositions rely on the column arriving in the same order as the rows, and the eng one additionally requires that no row be dropped -- it advances the key column and the row list together and would misalign on the first skipped element. That order-and-count guarantee is what row 4 proves, and it is the only thing these three need from the verb.
row-5-emergence.eng: Group-by is a projection plus an accumulator. Every database does it with a hash rather than an alist, and the shape is identical.
row-5-emergence.math: Successive differences turn a sequence into its discrete derivative, and the sign of that derivative is monotonicity. It is the cheapest sortedness check there is.
row-5-emergence.cs: A frequency histogram over a projected column is the first thing anyone runs on a log file, and it is four lines once the projection has a name.
